title: Bira 91 Founder Ankur Jain Exits After Two-Year Standoff, Surrenders 17.8% Stake to Investors
excerpt: The craft beer pioneer signed a settlement with lenders and institutional shareholders, ending a bitter dispute marked by unpaid salaries, employee protests, and halted production.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Ankur Jain resigned from B9 Beverages, surrendering a 17.8% stake and all executive powers.
  • The settlement ends a two-year dispute with major investors and lenders over unpaid salaries and halted production.
  • B9 Beverages' debt nears ₹1,000 crore, with revenue dropping from ₹824 crore to ₹638 crore in FY24.
  • Investors plan to inject ₹400 crore to recapitalize and restart operations within three to six months.

Ankur Jain, the founder who turned Bira 91 into India's most recognizable craft beer brand, has walked away from the company he built. In a settlement signed on Tuesday, Jain resigned from the board of B9 Beverages, gave up all executive powers, and agreed to surrender his family's entire 17.8% stake — ending a bitter, two-year standoff with investors and lenders that had left the company paralyzed.

The Settlement

Under the agreement, Jain and his family will be released from personal liabilities tied to the company, according to sources cited by the Economic Times. Jain had personally guaranteed some of B9 Beverages' loans. Both sides have agreed to withdraw all legal proceedings filed against each other.

"I am thankful to everyone who has allowed us to create the Bira 91 brand — team members, investors, business partners," Jain told the Economic Times. "We ran into rough weather in the last two years. However, with this resolution, the business will enter a new phase of growth—a phase in which I will be cheering for the company and the brand from the sidelines."

How It Unraveled

Bira 91 was India's craft beer success story. Founded in 2015, the brand positioned itself as a premium alternative to mass-market lagers, resonating with urban millennials and quickly expanding to multiple countries. The company attracted heavyweight backers — Peak XV Partners (formerly Sequoia India), Japanese beverage giant Kirin Holdings, Belgian investor Sofina, and Sixth Sense Ventures. At its peak, B9 Beverages was valued at roughly $625 million.

But the finances told a different story. Revenue fell from ₹824 crore in FY23 to ₹638 crore in FY24, while losses ballooned from ₹445 crore to ₹749 crore. Debt climbed toward ₹1,000 crore. Production was halted around September 2025, and the company has not brewed beer since.

"Salary delays as a result of financial mismanagement have run into several crores. There is also vendor pressure and the risk of insolvency proceedings."

— Source familiar with B9 Beverages' situation, speaking to Mint

Employee Protests and Unpaid Wages

The human cost was severe. Of roughly 900 employees at the company's peak, about 400 roles were phased out through 2025. Around 80 employees reportedly continued working without pay, including factory workers and mid-management staff. Former employees alleged that provident fund and TDS amounts were deducted but never deposited.

In early 2026, about 50 former employees protested outside Jain's Delhi residence over unpaid salaries and statutory dues. Over 250 employees had earlier petitioned the board and top investors demanding Jain's removal, citing "corporate governance failure, lack of transparency, delays in employee dues and salaries."

What Happens Next

With Jain gone, existing investors plan to infuse approximately ₹400 crore at a significantly reduced valuation, with an option for an additional ₹100 crore. A new CEO is expected to be appointed, and the company aims to resume operations within three to six months.

Whether Bira 91 can stage a comeback remains an open question. The brand retains strong consumer recognition, but the Indian craft beer market has evolved rapidly in Bira's absence, with competitors filling the vacuum. The company will also need to rebuild relationships with vendors, distributors, and a workforce that was publicly burned.

For India's startup ecosystem, the Bira saga joins a growing list of cautionary tales about venture-backed consumer brands that scaled faster than their unit economics could support—a lesson that resonates well beyond the craft beer category.
